# How to use this editorial

For each problem, identify the reduction before reading the code. The proof paragraph names the invariant that should have appeared in your own derivation.

# A. Exam Room Bounds

Create source-to-group edges fixed at each demand, allowed unit group-to-room edges, room-to-sink bounded edges, and a sink-to-source edge fixed at total demand. This is a bounded circulation, so the balance reduction decides feasibility.

## How to find it

Rows and columns are two sides of a bipartite unit-flow model. Row demands are
fixed source-edge flows, room limits are lower/upper sink-edge bounds, and an
allowed pair is a unit middle edge. Fixing the return edge to the total demand
turns the whole construction into a circulation.

## Correctness

A valid selection sends one unit through exactly each selected pair; row and
column constraints become the stated edge bounds, so it produces a feasible
circulation. Conversely, integral max flow makes every middle edge zero or
one. Reading its unit edges gives distinct allowed choices, with exact row
degrees and bounded column degrees. The bounded-circulation equivalence then
decides the instance exactly.

## Complexity and tests

The graph has `R+C+4` vertices and `E+R+C+O(1)` edges. Test duplicate-looking
constraints, a room minimum unreachable from enough groups, zero row demands,
and feasible totals whose allowed-pair structure is nevertheless impossible.

# B. Bounded Exact Shipment

Add a fixed return edge `t -> s` carrying exactly `F`. The requested shipment
is now a circulation. For every bounded edge, pre-send its lower bound, record
the resulting vertex imbalances and its mandatory cost, and retain capacity
`high-low`.

Connect a super-source to positive-imbalance vertices and negative-imbalance
vertices to a super-sink. A minimum-cost flow saturating all super-source edges
repairs conservation at minimum additional cost. If it cannot send the total
imbalance, the shipment is impossible.

The lower-bound transformation is bijective: subtracting lower flows maps every
feasible exact shipment to one repairing flow, and adding them back reverses
the map. Costs differ only by the recorded mandatory constant, so minimum cost
is preserved. With at most the total imbalance augmentations, the SPFA-based
reference runs in `O(FVE)` for these small flow bounds.

# C. Selective Quota Profit

Send only `K` units from the source through worker vertices. Worker capacity one
means a worker is selected at most once; eligibility edges choose a project.
Project-to-sink capacity enforces upper quotas. Give the first `low[j]` slots a
reward `-BIG`, then verify that every rewarded slot was used.

## How to find it

The flow value performs the selection: unused workers simply carry no flow.
Eligibility costs are negative profits. `BIG` exceeds the complete possible
profit difference, making lower-quota satisfaction lexicographically prior to
profit maximization.

## Correctness

Every integral value-`K` flow selects exactly `K` distinct workers and one
eligible project for each. Conversely every valid selective assignment gives
such a flow. Upper capacities and verified mandatory slots enforce both quota
bounds. After removing the constant reward, minimizing cost is exactly
maximizing assignment profit.

## Complexity and tests

There are `O(n+p)` vertices and `O(n+m+p)` edges and `K` augmentations. Test
`K=0`, workers left unused, tight quotas, and infeasible lower quotas.

# D. Bounded Convex Allocation

First assign every machine its lower bound. For machine `i`, the cost of its
`j`-th additional unit is

```text
a[i] * (2 * (low[i] + j) - 1) + b[i].
```

These marginal costs form an increasing arithmetic sequence. The remaining
task is to select the globally smallest `K-sum(low)` marginals, respecting the
finite length of each sequence.

## How to find it

For a threshold `T`, count in constant time how many terms of one arithmetic
sequence are at most `T`. Summing this over machines gives a monotone predicate.
Binary-search the first threshold covering the required count, sum every term
strictly below it with the arithmetic-series formula, then take the remaining
tied terms at the threshold.

## Correctness

Discrete convexity makes each machine's marginals nondecreasing, so any optimal
allocation using `x` extra units from it uses its first `x` marginals. Thus
allocations correspond exactly to prefix selections from these sequences.
Selecting all values below the smallest covering threshold and any required
tied values is precisely the globally cheapest such selection.

## Complexity and tests

Threshold counting costs `O(n)` and needs `O(log C)` iterations, where `C` is
the marginal-value range. Memory is `O(n)`. Test infeasible totals, negative
marginals, nonzero lower bounds, huge capacities, and many equal marginals.

# E. Exact Red Forest

Price every red edge by `lambda`. Kruskal, stopped after
`n-components` accepted edges, solves the penalized fixed-size forest problem.
The red count is nonincreasing in `lambda`; opposite tie rules give the extreme
red counts among equally optimal forests.

## How to find it

The difficult condition is the exact red count. A forest with the requested
component count has fixed size, so truncated Kruskal is still the optimizer
after adding a charge per red edge.

## Correctness

Fixed-size forests are bases of a truncated graphic matroid. Its exchange
property gives the same tie interval as for spanning trees: all red counts
between the two optimal tie extremes are attainable. Binary search finds the
boundary price whose interval contains `k`; subtracting `lambda*k` recovers
the minimum original weight.

## Complexity and tests

Each price evaluation sorts `m` edges, giving `O(m log m log W)`. Test zero
selected edges, disconnected graphs with enough forest rank, impossible color
counts, negative weights, and many modified-cost ties.

# F. Congested Team Assignment

Worker-to-team edges contribute negative profit. Replace team cost a*x^2 by x unit slots with marginal costs a(2k-1). Reward the mandatory lower-quota slots by -BIG and verify them afterward. A single exact min-cost flow now optimizes assignment and congestion together.

## How to find it

This is assignment flow except the price of a team depends on its final load.
Convexity makes the dependence separable: the `k`-th member costs the marginal
`a[j](2k-1)`. Replace one nonlinear team edge by ordered unit slot edges, and
use the lower-quota reward from the quota problem on its first slots.

## Correctness

An integral value-`n` flow chooses one eligible team per specialist. Since a
team's marginal slot costs are nondecreasing, any cheapest flow using `x`
slots uses precisely the first `x`; their sum is `a[j]x^2`. The `-BIG` reward,
chosen larger than the full real-objective range, makes saturation of every
lower-quota slot lexicographically prior to profit and congestion. After the
explicit saturation check, feasible flows and valid assignments correspond
bijectively and have equal real objective, so the returned maximum is exact.

## Complexity and tests

There are `O(n+p)` vertices and `O(m+n+sum high)` edges, with at most `n`
augmentations. Test zero congestion, tight project sizes, a quota forcing an
unprofitable assignment, equal marginal slots, and infeasible eligibility.
